lawyer:
Shamsul Huq Chowdhury with Ali Akbar, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner.
Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with MA Rouf, Mirza Hussain Haider, SM Monir, Advocates ----- For the Respondent No. 4. 
Syed JR Modassir Hossain, DAG ----- For the Respondent No.1.
parties:
Saifur Rahman ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, Dhaka and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Naimuddin Ahmed J : In this Writ Petition arising out of an application under Article 102 of the Constitution an order passed by the Government, the respondent No. 1, under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 (Annexure 'H') whereby the settlement of certain lands granted to the petitioner by the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola, some time in 1951, was cancelled and the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola, was directed to take steps for recognizing the respondent No. 4 and some others as co-tenants of those lands, and an order passed by the Government under Memo No. 11-1/86/438/1(3) dated 19.11.86 (Annexure 'J) whereby an application for review filed to the Government by the petitioner for reviewing the order contained in the memo first above mentioned was rejected, have been called in question.

2. The facts leading to this Writ Petition are somewhat lengthy.

3. It is alleged by, the petitioner that three plots of lands appertaining to RS Plot Nos. 557, 558 & 559 comprising a total area of 1261.95 acres corresponding to CS Plots Nos. 521 and 522 in the CS record of right were the lands of mauza Char Sitaram and were the khan lands of the Crown. These lands were lost by diluvian in the river, Tetulia, and during the RS operations conducted in the year, 1941, these lands were shown as river blocks outside the revenue survey. After remaining under the river, Tetulia, for over 20 years, these lands re-appeared in the year, 1951, and became vested in the Government. Thereafter, the Khasmahal Authorities of the then District of Bakerganj (now the District of Bhola) granted settlement of these lands with the petitioner and others in Miscellaneous Case No. 274 of 1947. The petitioner and other lessees, after due execution of their respective Kabuilyats, entered into possession therein. While the petitioner and his other co-tenants were in peaceful possession of these lands, one Rafiqul Huq Chowdhury made a claim over these lands as his own lands and tried to dispossess the petitioner. Having failed to enter into possession of these lands the said Rafiqul Huq Chowdhury filed an application before the then Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Bhola, with a prayer for drawing up a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The learned Sub-Divisional Magistrate drew up a proceeding and the present petitioner and others who were the opposite parties therein appeared and after hearing both the parties the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, by an order dated 3.1.57, found the petitioner and his co-tenants in possession of these lands and also found the said Rafiqul Huq Chowdhury out of possession, and, accordingly, declared the possession of the petitioner and his cotenants in the said lands. Against this judgment and order dated 3.1.57 a Criminal Motion being Criminal Motion No. 11(1) of 1957 was filed before the Sessions Judge, Bakerganj, by the respondent No. 4 of this writ petition. The said Criminal Motion was heard by the Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Bakerganj, and by his judgment and order dated 31.8.57 he dismissed the Criminal Motion. Against this decision of the Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Bakerganj, a revisional application being Criminal Revision No. 547 of 1957 was preferred before the High Court of East Pakistan, as it was then. The High Court also rejected the said revisional application upholding the order of the Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Bakerganj. The respondent No. 4 and his party-men then instituted a Title Suit being Title Suit No. 191 of 1959 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Barisal, claiming only 75.00 acres of lands out of RS Plot Nos. 557, 558 and 559 with a prayer for establishment of title and khan possession. The present petitioner and the respondent No. 1, the Government of East Pakistan, as it was then, were made parties in the said suit. The respondent No. 1, the Government of East Pakistan, appeared and contested the suit disclaiming the alleged title of the respondent No. 4. The present petitioner also contested the suit by filing a separate written statement. A prayer was made in the said suit by the present petitioner and other defendants for temporary injunction for restraining the plaintiffs of that suit including the respondent No. 4 of this writ petition from entering into the disputed lands. The injunction matter was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Barisal, and by his order dated 17.11.60 restrained the respondent No. 4 and other plaintiffs of that suit from entering into the disputed lands till the disposal of the suit. Thereafter, the Title Suit abated on 3rd April, 1973 under the provisions of President's Order Nos. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 at the instance of the Government. As against the order of abatement a revisional application was filed before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court. This revisional application was allowed setting aside the abatement order and the suit was restored and remanded for trial to the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Bhola, and it was then re-numbered as Title Suit No. 10 of 1984. On 2.12.84 the respondent No. 4 preferred an application under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 151 of the Code praying for temporary injunction against the defendant No. 1 in the said suit (the Deputy Commissioner of Bhola), who is the respondent No. 3 in this Writ Petition, for restraining him from disturbing their alleged possession in the disputed lands and also for restraining him from obstructing them from harvesting the paddy standing thereon. The Defendant No. 1, the Deputy Commissioner of Bhola, contested the application for temporary injunction by filing a written objection wherein he denied title and possession of the plaintiffs in the disputed lands. By an order dated 11.12.84 the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the prayer for temporary injunction restraining the said defendant No. 1 from disturbing the alleged possession of the plaintiffs of that suit and from interfering with harvesting the paddy standing thereon by them. An appeal was preferred against the order of the learned Subordinate Judge, Bhola, before the District Judge, Bhola and this appeal was numbered as Misc. Appeal No. 71 of 1984. The learned District Judge heard the aforesaid appeal and by his judgment and order dated 31.1.85 affirmed the order dated 11.12.84 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and dismissed the said appeal. Thereafter a revisional application was filed before the High Court Division, Barisal Bench, against the order of the learned District Judge on 31.1.85 in which Rule was issued and it was numbered as Civil Revision No. 25 of 1985. After hearing this revisional application the High Court Division, by an order dated 29.5.85, set aside the judgment and order passed by the District Judge on 31.1.85 and also the order passed by the Subordinate Judge on 11.12.84 and rejected the application for temporary injunction. As against this order of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court dated 29.5.85 an application for Special Leave to Appeal was preferred before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court and this appeal was registered as Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 149 of 1985. After hearing the parties the learned Appellate Division of the Supreme Court by its judgment and order dated 8.7.85, dismissed the petition upholding the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division of the Supreme Court after finding, it is alleged, that the Court did not find possession of the plaintiffs in the disputed lands.

4. Having thus failed to achieve their purpose the respondent No. 4 and his party-men filed an application before the respondent No. 3, the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola, and obtained an order in their favour passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.), Bhola, on 17.11.84 in Misc. Case No. 125 of 1984-85 and against this order the petitioner of this writ petition filed an application before the respondent No. 3, the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola, and on the basis of this application the respondent No. 3, the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola, by his order dated 28.11.84, directed the Magistrate-in-charge of the local police camp to ensure peaceful possession and harvesting of the paddy by the petitioner as a result of which the petitioner and others could peacefully harvest the crops grown by them in the disputed lands.

5. Thereafter, the respondent No. 4 filed an application, on 2.1.86 before the respondent No. 1, the Secretary of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, claiming title and possession in these lands. The respondent No: 1 asked the Deputy Lands Reforms Commissioner to hold an enquiry and submit a report. No notice of any such enquiry was served on the petitioner and others and it was reported that the Deputy Land Reforms Commissioner came to Bhola and visited the disputed lands on 19.2.86 accompanied by the Upazila Revenue Officer, Bhola, and held an enquiry from 18.2.86 to 20.2.86 and then submitted a biased report holding that these lands did not appertain to Char Sitaram and had been wrongly settled by the Khasmahal Authorities with the petitioner and others in the year, 1951. On the basis of this report the respondent No. 1 passed the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/438/1(3) dated 19.11.86 cancelling the settlement granted to the petitioner by the Khasmahal Authorities in the year, 1951, and also directing to recognise the respondent No. 4 and others as tenants of the disputed lands. No notice was served on the petitioner and he was not heard by the respondent No. 1 before passing this order. On hearing about this order the petitioner filed an application before the respondent No. 1 for review of the order on various grounds and this application was also rejected by the Respondent No. 1 by his order dated 19.11.86 confirming the order dated 5.11.86. As against these orders passed by the Respondent No. 1 that the petitioner approached this Court and obtained the present Rule.

6. The Respondent No. 1, the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, has filed an affidavit-in-opposition denying the allegations made by the petitioner. Briefly stated, the case of the respondent No. 1 is, that the three disputed plots, namely, plot Nos. 557, 558 and 559 never appertained to Char Sitaram. These three plots appertained to mouza Udaypur which belonged to the ex-rent-receivers namely, the Landlords of Ulania and the Bhuban Mohan Roy Chowdhury Estate, and as such, the settlement of these lands with the petitioner and his co-tenants by the Khas Mahal Authorities was illegal. It has also been stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that the petitioner has no title in these lands. An application was made by the Respondent No. 4 to the respondent No. 1 for holding an enquiry into the matter. An order was then passed directing enquiry by the Deputy Land Reforms Commissioner. The Deputy Land Reforms Commissioner held a detailed enquiry into the disputed lands and submitted a report opining that these three plots appertained to mouza Udaypur and not to mouza Char Sitaram. The Deputy Land Reforms Commissioner also opined that these lands belonged to two sets of ex-rent-receivers mentioned above. On the basis of this report and after hearing the parties the respondent No. 1 passed the impugned orders which were based on sound reasons.

7. The respondent No. 4 also entered appearance and contested the writ petition by filing an affidavit-in-opposition wherein, apart from general denial of the statements of the petitioner made in the writ petition, it has been contended that the three disputed RS plots were never part of mouza Char Sitaram. It has also been contended that these three disputed plots were part of mouza Udaypur belonging to the estates of the Landlords of Ulania and Bhuban Mohan Roy Chowdhury. After re-appearance of these lands from diluvian these ex-landlords entered into possession of these lands and granted settlement thereof with the respondent No. 4 and others. The respondent No. 4 also contends that since the settlement was made the respondent No. 4 and others have been possessing these lands peacefully. While admitting that one Rafiqul Huq Chowdhury filed a proceeding milder section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against the petitioner he contends that he was not a party in the said proceeding and as such, he was not bound by any order passed therein. He also contends that while he along with his co-tenants was in possession in these plots, the Khasmahal Officer of Bhola tried to have these plots wrongly recorded within mouza Char Sitaram during the SA operations and as such, he instituted Title Suit No. 191 of 1959 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Bakerganj, against the Government, the petitioner of this Writ Petition and others who were defendants Nos. 2-110. This suit is still pending after having been re-numbered as Title Suit No. 10 of 1984 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Bhola. While the respondent No. 4 and others were in peaceful possession of these plots the petitioner and his party-men tried to disturb their possession and as such, the respondent No. 4 and other co-tenants filed an application before, the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue) Bhola and after hearing the parties the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue), Bhola passed an order on 17.11.84 in their favour. Thereafter, the present petitioner and other defendants of Title Suit No. 10 of 1984 filed Misc. Case No. 125 of 1984-85 before the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola and the Deputy Commissioner in collusion with the petitioner and his party-men passed an order on 28.11.84 directing a Magistrate, who was in charge in the police camp in the locality, to ensure possession of the disputed lands and harvesting of the paddy by the petitioner and his party-men who has taken settlement from the i3overnment and on the basis of this order, the petitioner and his party men forcibly harvested paddy from .50 acres of lands out of the three disputed 1Dlots. The respondent No. 4 then filed and (application before the Subordinate Judge, Bhola, in (title Suit No. 10 of 1984, praying for restraining the Deputy Commissioner of Bhola from deploying t any police force in the disputed lands and the prayer was allowed. There was an appeal against the order of the Subordinate Judge before the District Judge, 13hola, and the District Judge affirmed the order of the Subordinate Judge. The orders of the Subordinate nudge and the District Judge were set aside by the relight Court Division of the Supreme Court, Barisal Bench, in Civil Revision No. 25 of 1985. Azoetition for special leave to appeal against the order 2A. the High Court Division before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court being Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 149 of 1985 was also dismissed. The respondent No. 4 then filed an application on 2.1.86 before the respondent No. 1 and the respondent No. 1 directed the Deputy Lands Reforms Commissioner to hold an enquiry into the matter and submit a report. Accordingly, the Deputy Lands Reforms Commissioner visited the disputed land on 19.2.86 and submitted his report on 25.6.86 finding that the three disputed plots were parts of Char Sitarammouza, that granting settlement of these plots by the Khasmahal Authorities to the petitioner and others in the year, 1951, was done wrongly and illegally and that the respondent No. 4 and his party-men were the bonafide tenants in those plots. On the basis of this report and after considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the respondent No. 1 passed an order contained in Memo No. 11-1/86/438/1(3) dated 19.11.86 cancelling the settlement granted to the petitioner and his other co-tenants and directing the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola, to take steps for recognising the respondent No. 4 and others as bonafide tenants of these plots. It is also stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that the petitioner filed an application for review against the order under the aforesaid memo and this application for review was also rejected by the respondent No. 1 under Memo No. 11-1/86/438/1(3) dated 19.11.86. The aforesaid orders are absolutely lawful orders and, as such, cannot be interfered with.

8. Subsequently, the petitioner filed 2 affidavits-in-reply to the affidavits-in-opposition submitted by the respondent No. 1 and the affidavit-in-opposition submitted by the respondent No. 4 and in these affidavits-in-reply the facts narrated in the original petition have been re-iterated.

9. Mr. Shamsul Huq Chowdhury, the learned. Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, first of all, attacked the impugned Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 on the ground that before passing this order whereby a right vested in the petitioner had been taken away, no notice was issued to him and he was not heard and as such, this order was in violation of the basic principles of natural justice.

10. The second ground taken by Mr. Chowdhury is that the respondent No. 1, or the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms or the Joint Secretary of the said Ministryis not empowered to pass the impugned order and in exercising the power with which they are not vested in law they acted arbitrarily and without jurisdiction.

11. The next ground of attack on the impugned orders by Mr. Chowdhury appears to be that when admittedly a litigation between the parties including the respondent No. 1 was pending in a court of competent jurisdiction to decide the issues in question it was not open to a party to the said litigation to take any step to the detriment of another party to the litigation. Mr. Syed JR Modassir Hossain, the Deputy Attorney-General, representing the respondent No. 1, argued, at first, that the respondent No. 1 was quite competent and empowered in view of section 146 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951, to pass an order revising the order passed by a Revenue Authority and as such it cannot be said that the impugned orders were incompetent and without jurisdiction.

12. He has also argued that it was always open to the respondent No. 1, the Government of Bangladesh, to rectify and modify any order it deemed to have been wrongly passed by any officer subordinate to it.

13. He has also contended that the order of the respondent No. 1 being passed on an enquiry report submitted by a competent officer of the Government was passed on objective materials and, as such, was not arbitrary or biased.

14. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate, representing the respondent No. 4, contended that the respondent No. 1 was vested under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 with the power to pass such orders as the impugned orders.

15. He also contended that the pendency of the litigation between the parties in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Bhola, could not be treated as a the against the right of the respondent No. 1 to rectify any error committed by any Officer appointed by the Respondent No. 1 and, as such, no exception can be taken to the impugned order on this ground.

16. Mr. Ahmed also contended that the order granting settlement to the petitioner and his co-tenants in 1951 by the Khasmahal Authorities being ability void the question of providing any opportunity to the petitioner to show cause against the impugned order cancelling the said settlement o, not arise as no question of natural justice was involved in such a case.

17. He, last of all, argued that in this writ petition vital disputed questions of facts are involved and as such this writ petition is not maintainable.

18. So far as the first ground taken by Mr. Chowdhury that before passing the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86, which is virtually the impugned order, no notice was issued on him and he was not afforded any opportunity by the authorities of showing cause against the impugned order and of being heard by the respondent No. 1, is concerned, it is necessary to refer to the relevant portion of this order which is at Annexure 'H' and which runs as follows :

"There is no factual and documentary proof to treat these plots of Char Udaypurmouza as belonging to Char Sitaram which is under Lalmohan Upazila and disturb the petitioner tenants who had taken settlement from the ex-landlords of the Ulania-Joint Estate and Bhuban Mohan Roy Chowdhury Estate as far back as in 1950. That these plots belonged to Char Udaypurmouza and not Char Sitaram was a settled issue decided upon by the Assistant Settlement Officer and Objection Officer during last S.A. operation against which no appeal was preferred by the local administration.

2. The Government in the Ministry have, therefore, decided that :

(a) the disputed land in plots No. 557, 558 and 559 be treated as belonging to mouza Udaypur in lawful recognition of the existing records of rights, both RS and SA and admitted to be forming part of Touzi No. 2872 belonging to the Ulania Joint Estate and Bhuban Mohan Roy Chowdhury Estate before the State Acquisition.

(b) The Settlement of the Lands given by the Local Administration by treating the same as Government khas land and forming part of mauza Char Sitaram has been illegal and is, therefore, cancelled.

(c) The petitioner along with others claim to have taken settlement of these lands from the ex-proprietors. They were also in possession of 3 the lands until ousted therefrom by police force deputed by the District Administration.

The petitioners should, therefore, be recognised as tenants by the Local Revenue Authority after scrutiny and examination of their papers and also after withdrawal of the TS Case No. 10/84 pending in the Court of Sub-Judge, Bhola."

The aforesaid letter was addressed by the .respondent No. 1 to the Deputy Commissioner, 1Bhola. A perusal of the above letter shows that certain findings were recorded adversely affecting the linterests claimed by the petitioner in the disputed plots. It further appears that the settlement on the ,basis of which the plaintiff has been claiming title in these plots was cancelled by the respondent No. 1. It also appears that the respondent No. 1 directed some other persons including the respondent No. 4 to be recognised as lawful tenants in these plots under the Government. There is no doubt that these observations and the order of the respondent No. 1, adversely affected the interest claimed by the petitioner in the disputed plots since this order sought to take away some rights and title with which the petitioner claims to have been vested in the disputed plots on the basis of his alleged settlement from the Government. As such, the petitioner was certainly entitled to be heard before he order was passed, because, to take away one's right denying one the right to be heard is to deny one natural justice. It is not disputed that no opportunity if hearing was offered to the petitioner before passing the impugned order on 5.6.86. We are therefore, of the opinion that the principles of natural justice were not observed before the order Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 was passed by respondent No. 1. It is difficult at this stage to accept the contention of Mr. Ahmed that the settlement alleged to have been granted to the petitioner in the year, 1951, by the Khasmahal Authorities was void and as such, the petitioner was not entitled to be heard before cancelling a void order. It cannot be said that the alleged settlement vas ex facie void. The question of vires of the alleged settlement of the petitioner cannot be decided within the limited scope of writ jurisdiction as it would involve detailed investigation into various questions of fact which can only be decided by a Court of competent jurisdiction. So, we are unable to accept the proposition that no question of the principles of natural justice was involved when the respondent No. 1 dealt with the matter. In these views of the matter, we are of opinion that the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 (Annexure 'H') cannot be supported in law as it was passed in utter disregard of the principle, "Audi alteram partem."

19. Mr. Shamsul Huq Chowdhury then attacked the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 contending that the Government was not authorised under any provision of law and was, therefore, not competent to make the impugned order rescinding the order of the Revenue Officer granting settlement to the petitioner and his alleged co-tenants. In this connection, Mr. Chowdhury drew our attention to sections 147, 148, 149 and 150 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 which provide for appeal, revision and review of the orders passed by the Revenue Officers under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. We carefully perused sections 147, 148, 149 and 150 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Section 147 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, provides for preferring appeal against the orders of the Revenue Officers and this section shows that the Appellate Authority is the Collector, when the order is made by a Revenue Officer subordinate to the Collector, Commissioner of the division, when the order is made by the Collector of a district within the division and the Board of Land Administration, when the order is made by the Commissioner of a division. There is no other authority under section 147 to whom an appeal can be preferred. Section 148 provides for the period of limitation for an appeal under section 147. Section 149 provides for revision of an order passed by a Revenue Officer. Under this section, similar to an appeal, the Collector, the Commissioner and the Board of Land Administration have been vested with power of revision against the orders 0f the Revenue Officers. Section 149 does not empower the Government to revise, rescind or cancel any order passed by a Revenue Officer. Section 150 provides for review of an order by the Officer himself who passed the order.

<u>20. From the above, it appears that the Board of Land Administration is the final authority to entertain appeal and revision against any order passed under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 by a Revenue Officer which includes an order granting settlement of land vested in the Government as in the case of settlement to the petitioner done by a regular proceeding under section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.</u>

<u>21. Mr. Syed JR Modassir Hossain, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, tried to rely on sub-section (1) of section 146 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and tried to argue that the general power of superintendence and control over the Revenue Officers empowers the Government to pass any order revising an order passed by a Revenue Officer. Sub-section (1) of section 146 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, as amended by Ordinance XXI of 1982 provides as follows :</u>

<u>"146(1) The general superintendence and control over all Revenue Officers shall be vested in and all such officers shall be subordinate to, the Board of Land Administration."</u>

<u>Section 146(1), therefore, shows that the general power of superintendence and control over all Revenue _Officers is vested in the Board of Land Administration and not in the Government. Moreover section 146(1) vests the Board of Land Administration with administrative control over the Revenue Officers and by no means empowers it to revise the orders passed by the Revenue Officers under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The powers of appeal, revision and review are in sections 147 to 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The power in section 146 does not, therefore, include the power to revise the orders of a Revenue Officer and this aspect of the legal position was candidly accepted by Mr. Ahmed while arguing for the respondent No. 4. Nothing has been placed before us to show that the Government is empowered under any provision of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, to cancel or rescind any order passed by the Revenue Authorities. Consequently, there is no substance in the submission made by the learned Deputy Attorney-General.</u>

22. It, therefore, appears that the submissions made by Mr. Chowdhury that the Government was not empowered under any provision of law to pass the impugned order and revise the order passed by the Revenue Officer granting settlement to the petitioner and his co-tenants has substance. So the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 passed by the Respondent No. 1 being passed by authority not vested by law to make such order suit without lawful authority.

24. Lastly, Mr. Chowdhury submitted that by passing the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 the respondent No. 1 sought to settle a dispute pending before a Civil Court of competent jurisdiction. In Title Suit No. 10 of 1984 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Bhola, precisely, the same question of law and fact are involved and in this suit the respondent No. 1 is also a party. As such Mr, Chowdhury wanted to say, the respondent No. 1 who is a party to the dispute which is sub judice before the Civil Court was not, in all fairness, entitled to take any action to the detriment of another party to the said litigation.

25. In relation to the last submission of Mr. Chowdhury it is necessary to refer to certain undisputed facts. One Rafiqul Huq Chowdhury, an alleged co-tenant of the respondent No. 4, filed a case under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure claiming title and possession in the disputed plots on the same basis as the respondent No. 4. The copy of the order of the learned Magistrate in this proceeding is at Annexure 'A' to the Writ Petition. This order was passed as far back as on 3.1.57 and its concluding portion runs as follows : "From all these above facts and circumstances and from the evidence on record, I find that the disputed land appertains to Char Sitaram (Block 'B') and not Udaypur as alleged by the 1st party and I am satisfied that the 2nd party and 3rd party were in possession of the proceeding land at the date of the order u/s 145 CrPC and it is, hereby, declared by this that the 2nd party and the 3rd party are entitled to possession thereof until evicted therefrom in due course of law.

Any disturbance of such possession until such eviction is also forbidden by law."

26. The present petitioner was one of the third parties in the above proceeding. The respondent No. 4 was not, however, a party to the said proceeding and as such, the order in this proceeding did not bind him, but it is relevant at least as evidence of possession of the petitioner at the time when the order was passed. The order in this proceeding was unsuccessfully challenged in Criminal Motion No.111(1) of 1957 before the learned Sessions Judge, Bakerganj, and ultimately before the High Court in Criminal Revision No. 547 of 1957. Thereafter, the respondent No. 4 instituted Title Suit No. 191 of 1959 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal, against the petitioner and others for establishment of title and khas possession in the disputed lands and this suit is still pending as Title Suit No. 10 of 1984 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Bhola. In this suit the petitioner and others filed an application for injunction for restraining the respondent No. 4 and the other plaintiffs of that suit from entering on the disputed lands and this application was allowed and the respondent No. 4 and the other plaintiffs were restrained from entering into the disputed lands by an order dated 17.11.60 as at Annexure 'C'. The respondent No. 4 then filed an application for temporary injunction against the respondent No. 3, the Deputy Commissioner of Bhola, who was the defendant No. 1 in that suit, for restraining him from disturbing the alleged possession of the respondent No. 4 and the prayer was allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge and the order of the Subordinate Judge was affirmed by the learned District Judge. The orders of the Subordinate Judge and the District Judge were reversed by the High Court Division of the Supreme Court in Civil Revision No. 25 of 1985 on 29.5.85 and the prayer of the respondent No. 4 was rejected finding that the respondent No. 4 and the other plaintiffs of the suit had no possession in the disputed lands till 1960. A petition for special leave to appeal being Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 149 of 1985 was filed before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court and was rejected by their Lordships of the Appellate Division. The order is at Annexure "E". His Lordship Shahabuddin Ahmed, J, as his Lordship was then, speaking for the Court observed "Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioner, has made strenuous efforts to convince us that the petitioners have been in possession all along on the basis of their settlement from the Ulania Joint Estate. But we find no evidence of any settlement from the ex-landlords. The suit land was recorded as Government khas land. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed contends that this entry in the khatian is wrong in that the suit land was found by the Settlement Officer and the Pleader Commissioner to be included in "Udaypur Mouza." But whether the land falls within Udaypurmouza or Char Sitarammouza, there is no dispute about its identity and it is found to be the one and the same land, which is the bone of contention between the parties. In the absence of any prima facie prbof of the settlement from the ex-landlords, the petitioners are trying to make out a case that if the land appertains to Udaypurmouza it will necessarily follow that it was the former Zaminders to the petitioners (sic.) As to possession, in a previous proceeding under section 145 CrPC MR Case No. III of 1954 lessees of the Zaminders were not found in possession. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed contends that in that proceeding the petitioners were not parties; but there is no dispute that the said proceeding was instituted in respect of this very land though it was filed by another set of claimants, and it is after the disposal of this proceeding that these petitioners filed the Title Suit claiming title and possession in respect of the same land. In these circumstances, the High Court Division prima facie found that the plaintiffs got no possession in the suit land and on that finding set aside the order of temporary injunction. We do not find any wrong in the finding of the High Court Division."

27. It is, therefore, clear that complicated and intricate question of title of the parties to the suit pending before the Civil Court is involved and this question of title can only be judicially resolved by a competent Court after due and proper consideration of the facts and law involved in the dispute. By the impugned order dated 5.6.86, the respondent No. 1 who is a party to the dispute pending in a competent Court virtually and substantially decided these disputed question of facts, law and title of the parties involved in the suit. The order of the respondent No. 1 also sought to frustrate the orders of the highest judicial forum in the country relating to the status quo of the parties in the disputed property during pendency of the suit in the Civil Court. Administrative interference by an incompetent authority in the matters pending for judicial determination, if encouraged, will augur the end of rule of law. Moreover, if a party to a litigation is allowed to take an action to the detriment of another party in respect of the subject-matter of the litigation it will be negation of the basic principles of administration of justice.

28. In the result, considering all the facts, circumstances and the submissions made by the learned Advocates we find that the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 is without lawful authority and of no legal effect. Consequently, the subsequent order under Memo No. 11-1/86/438/1(3) dated 19.11.86 which is virtually re-iteration of the former and direction to implement the former order is also without lawful authority.

29. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute. 30. The impugned orders passed under Memo No. 11-1/86-230 dated 5.6.86 and Memo No. 11-1/86/438/1(3) dated 19.11.86 as at Annexure 'H' and 'J' are declared to be without lawful authority and are of no legal effect.

There is no order as to cost.

End.
